nameStory: The feather blenny gets its name from its delicate, feathery fin rays that flutter gracefully in the water like tiny plumes. When you spot one perched on a rock or nestled in an oyster shell, those wispy fins give it an almost bird-like quality as they wave gently in the current.
description: The feather blenny is a small, slender fish that rarely grows longer than your index finger - about 4 inches at most. This little bottom-dweller has a elongated body with a blunt head and large, expressive eyes that seem almost too big for its face. Its most distinctive features are its delicate, thread-like fin rays that give it a soft, feathery appearance as it darts between rocks and oyster shells along the shore.

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Thread-like, feathery fin rays that flutter delicately in the water, giving the fish an almost wispy, ethereal appearance

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Slender, elongated body that feels smooth and slightly slimy to the touch, with a distinctive blunt head that looks oversized

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny fish, typically no longer than your index finger - usually 3-4 inches maximum length

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Disproportionately large, prominent eyes that give it an alert, almost curious expression

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Lives close to the bottom, often wedged into crevices in oyster reefs or rocky shores where it can quickly dart for cover

habitat: In New England waters, look for feather blennies around rocky shorelines and oyster beds in shallow coastal areas. They prefer areas with plenty of nooks and crannies where they can hide, often found in tide pools or just below the low tide line. These little fish love structured habitats like barnacle-covered rocks, mussel beds, and the shells of living oyster reefs.

seasonality.spring: More active as waters warm, beginning to move into shallower areas and becoming easier to spot during low tides.
seasonality.summer: Most active and visible during summer months when they're in peak condition, often seen darting between rocks in tide pools.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may begin moving to slightly deeper or more protected waters as temperatures start to drop.
seasonality.winter: Less visible and active, likely hiding deeper in crevices and rock formations to avoid the coldest water temperatures.

funFact: Despite being tiny, feather blennies are surprisingly bold and will fearlessly defend their small territories from fish many times their size, rushing out to chase away intruders before quickly darting back to safety!
confusionNotes: The feather blenny's delicate, thread-like fins immediately set it apart from other small coastal fish. Remember: if the fins look wispy and feathery rather than solid and triangular, you've likely found your blenny.
contextualKnowledge: This species was named after Nicholas Marcellus Hentz, likely a French-American scientist from Charleston who sent specimens to researchers in the 1800s. The scientific name reflects the old tradition of honoring people who contributed to natural history collections.
compareHints: Since the feather blenny is the only species in its genus found in New England waters, compare it to other blenny family members by looking for its distinctively feathery fins. Other blennies in the region tend to have more solid, less delicate fin rays and often different body proportions or coloration patterns.
